STATEMENT ON SHIPMENTS AND QUOTA POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a number of the members from western Canada have been asking me about grain quotas in Manitoba and in the central and eastern parts of Saskatchewan. I am now able to report that even though, because of ice conditions, navigation has not been officially opened at the lakehead, grain is now moving in substantial volume. Fourteen million bushels have now been shipped, of which 9.9 million bushels were wheat. These 14 million bushels compare with shipments to the same date last year of 10.4 million bushels. There are 15 vessels now loading grain at terminals at the lakehead with grain destined for eastern Canada and export markets.
It is expected that in the weeks ahead a substantial volume of grain will be shipped from the lakehead. This means that producers in western Canada at shipping points tributary to the lakehead can look forward to greatly improved delivery opportunities and a general rise in the quota level.

maintopic: STATEMENT ON SHIPMENTS AND QUOTA POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the minister should exert every influence to have an increased volume of grain moved eastward because of the very low delivery quotas in Manitoba and in parts of Saskatchewan, particularly the central and eastern parts. As of April 5 there were quotas of 2 bushels or less at 270 points in Manitoba as compared with only 58 in that position a year ago. In Saskatchewan 871 points had the very low quotas of 2 or 3 bushels as compared with 467 in that position a year ago.
I had hoped that the minister would have given the house more information, and I should like to ask him this question on the orders of the day. What is the objective for the quota at the end of the crop year? Is it the target of the government to have an equalized quota? If so, do they hope that the quota will be 7 bushels an acre, 8 bushels an acre, or what does the minister think the situation will be?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: STATEMENT ON SHIPMENTS AND QUOTA POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not the official spokesman with respect to agriculture on this side of
the house, but I could not resist the temptation to rise in connection with the announcement the minister has just made to indicate to him that while the announcement is most welcome, there is now every reason why an increase in the movement of grain, certainly eastward if not westward, can be expected because of the additional warehousing facilities that have been established on the St. Lawrence. I refer, of course, to Montreal where large extensions have been made, to Baie Comeau and, I believe, Sorel and Three Rivers.
There is one point I should like to bring to the attention of the minister. The former minister of trade and commerce when he was in office announced a reduction in the cost of moving grain of 3 cents per bushel, and I am wondering whether the government has given consideration to a further reduction. I do so because when the former minister made the announcement I think he gave some indication that the reduction might eventually be in the neighbourhood of 5 cents per bushel. I hope the government will find it possible to reduce freight costs to a greater extent than 3 cents per bushel.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday we heard the minister complain that in his opinion the decisions of the tariff board had done injury to the interests of Canadian producers in that their decisions had eroded the intention to give the necessary protection to those who were engaged in manufacturing in Canada as opposed to importing. speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member, but I would ask that he be given the attention of the house. It is rather difficult to hear and I am sure it is difficult for him to talk with so many conversations going on.

I believe it would be much more responsible, if the government of the day is not happy with the decisions of the tariff board, to find ways and means of altering the responsibility of that board or by replacing its existing members. I believe it ill behooves us to permit individuals to remain in office while continuing to attack and criticize their decisions.
We are most unhappy with the legislation now before us, and we intend to continue to expose and oppose it. We believe the effect of this legislation will be to add to the cost of consumer goods in Canada, and we are more particularly concerned because we believe it is a means whereby the cost of production in Canada is going to be increased beyond the high levels that these costs have already attained. We believe that investment in equipment and machinery in our major fields of endeavour in Canada plays a very important role in respect of the cost level of our production. We would hate to see anything done which would add to the heavy investment burden that is necessary, in this modern world of today, to supply employment to the Canadian people.
We believe this legislation will do that. We believe it will add to the amount of investment capital required to provide employment for our people. I do not believe the government has paid adequate attention to the representations of Canadian entrepreneurs respecting this legislation. I can easily understand the position taken yesterday by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, who is very closely associated with the major commercial enterprise in the Pacific west, namely the lumbering industry. At least this member of the House of Commons had read the submissions of such reputable organizations as the Vancouver board of trade and
Customs Tariff
others in regard to this legislation. All he was doing was, to the best of his ability, defending the interests of Canadian producers. We feel that not only will the consumers of this country be hit by having to pay higher prices but our producers, and especially our exporters, will suffer if this legislation really becomes effective. We believe it will have an adverse effect upon our trading position with other nations.
We look upon this legislation as nothing less than a back door approach on the part of the Tories in office to a return to high tariffs. In my opinion it again underlines what I have said on other occasions, namely that in the field of tariffs at least the Tories are producing ample evidence to indicate that they have learned nothing since the days when they were last in office, the days of the hungry thirties.
The minister is pleading for the passage of this measure in order to provide employment in Canada. It is our contention that this measure, as well as other like measures that he has introduced in the past, is directly responsible for increasing unemployment in our nation. We do not provide employment for our people by ostracizing ourselves from the markets of the world, by raising our costs of production and by raising our tariff walls. In so far as the over-all picture is concerned, what we do may supply relief to individual concerns or individuals, but it will aggravate the very difficult economic situation that now faces us. What will happen is that it will add to the already growing ranks of the unemployed.

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minisier of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak for just a few minutes and express some views on this legislation. I wish to point out at the beginning, as has been pointed out very ably on a number of occasions by the Minister of Finance in dealing with this matter in the house, that this proposed legislation is intended to relieve Canadian producers from unfair competition. It is not a device to give new protection to Canadian industry.
As we know, we have in Canada a customs tariff that has been established over the past 75 years by the various governments that have held office during that time. It is interesting to note that in the adjustments which have taken place in that tariff since this government took office, the number of specific items which have been reduced have outnumbered by quite a wide margin the number of items which have been increased.
So the opposition may not claim that I am urging higher tariffs in speaking on this measure, I should like to spend just a moment

Customs Tariff
to outline very briefly what I said on this matter when speaking to the Canadian Manufacturers' Association in Toronto on February 7. This is what I said:
Some people say the government should give greater protection to industry by raising tariffs against imports. Those who make this suggestion should realize that those against whom they would have us raise tariffs are also our customers for the exports on which we rely so heavily for our economic well-being. They must also realize that one out of every four Canadians is employed in either producing for, or shipping to, the export market. Those countries, against which they would have us raise tariffs, would certainly retaliate by increasing tariffs against our exports. And, for every Canadian who would be helped by raising tariffs, there would be at least one Canadian hurt by tariffs being raised against the products we export.
I think we must all realize that, if we are to continue to have high employment in Canada, we can only do so by industry producing products which will be competitive, and sell against competition.
These were the views I expressed on that occasion, and I have expressed them on numerous occasions since. They are still my views, Mr. Speaker.
The purpose of this legislation is simply to eliminate the loopholes in the act by which foreign producers can obtain an unfair advantage over their Canadian competitors, by making their products differ in some small technical detail. I think it is clear, Mr. Speaker, that there never was any intention in the minds of those who established our tariff during the past 75 years that this sort of tariff evasion should be possible. The unfair competition that has arisen by reason of these loopholes being there has had a detrimental effect on employment in Canada. I also think it is clear that if these anomalies are not removed, further deterioration in our employment picture will result.
The intent of the proposed changes is simply to give Canadian industry those levels of protection which previous parliaments intended. Again I say that our tariff was established, not by any one government, but by all governments that have held office during the past 75 years. Over the years, those governments intended that industry in Canada should be permitted to build up and prosper. It was for these reasons that certain tariffs were established. They have been agreed to by the various parliaments that have sat during this 75-year period. It was not the intention of the members who sat in this parliaments that those tariffs should be circumvented. The changes which are proposed in this legislation will greatly increase the incentive of Canadian producers to broaden the scope of their production and thereby increase employment.
The nagging opposition to this measure which has gone on in the eight days during

which this measure has been before parliament, I believe, Mr. Speaker, is a clear indication of where the opposition stand on the question of providing jobs for their fellow Canadians. They obviously want foreign producers to have all the loopholes possible to get their products into Canada at unfair rates of duty and so take orders which should be providing jobs for Canadians.

During the past few months I have been in Great Britain, the United States, France and Switzerland, and in talking to businessmen in these countries I have been dismayed to learn of the very alarming picture that has been built up in their minds by members of the opposition speaking here in parliament with respect to conditions in Canada. When I asked them where they got these impressions they said they heard reports over the radio and read newspaper accounts of speeches that had been made by members of parliament, and they were shocked at what these speeches indicated as to the state of our economy. I have been told by businessmen in all these countries that this kind of propaganda is having a very serious adverse effect on businessmen who are contemplating the establishment of plants in Canada which would provide jobs for Canadians.
I think it is obvious to all of us from talking to people in this country that the same kind of effect has been created in the minds of Canadian businessmen. When people in Canada who would otherwise be building plants and expanding inventories hear about

the picture of gloom and doom that is being painted in parliament, they are alarmed and have a tendency to delay their plans and not do the things they had otherwise intended to do. By their opposition to this measure hon. members on the other side of the house in my opinion have made it very clear that they are in favour of providing jobs for workers in other countries rather than for their fellow Canadians, as this legislation seeks to do.
This legislation simply enables Canadian products to receive the kind of protection that was intended for them by the various parliaments that over the years have established the rates of duty. The people who established these tariffs did not intend that by means of a slight variation, or a small change, a producer in another country could get around the tariff and bring in his product, varying only in some slight degree from the Canadian product, at a very low tariff rate or free of duty.
As these foreign producers are able to do this they are taking away a very large market from Canadian producers, and our producers are not given the confidence they should have to go ahead and expand their production and range of products because they fear that some foreign manufacturer can produce something almost the same and compete unfairly with the product they are producing or would like to produce. The very clearly demonstrated opposition to the bill before the house at the present time has the effect of doing everything possible to deny the right to work to Canadian workmen who would otherwise have jobs in plants manufacturing products that should be produced in Canada, and will be produced provided legislation such as that now before us is passed.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I think it is about time the opposition took a realistic and objective look at what they are doing. The time is long overdue for them to adopt a responsible attitude toward the welfare of their fellow Canadians. I think they should stop doing what they have been doing for quite some time, namely trying to paint a picture of doom and gloom in order to create what they would consider a satisfactory picture in preparation for the next election, and get down to a realistic view of what is needed here in Canada.
What we as Canadians must all do is everything we can to make it possible for every Canadian to have a job. The opposition should not spend its time trying to hold up measures directed toward this end, because by so doing, they are doing everything they can in favour of producers in other countries and the provision of jobs for foreign workmen rather than for Canadian workmen. He said that we on this side should not, in discussion of bills of this kind or, indeed, in the consideration of any economic question, indulge in criticism of the economy, or expose the weaknesses of government policy in respect of the serious problems facing that economy because if we do so we are indulging in doom and gloom.
The minister told us once again this afternoon that he has travelled throughout Europe, which is perfectly true, and throughout the United States, which is also perfectly true. He told us that he has talked to businessmen in Zurich, Paris and London, which is perfectly true; he spends a great deal of time travelling in foreign parts and talking to foreign businessmen. (b) whether goods are custom made to specifications, and whether adequate facilities exist in Canada for the economic production of such goods within a reasonable period of time.

Especially in this day and age of automation when industrialists are continually looking into ways and means of installing new machinery, much of it of a highly technical nature, I think it is far too great an imposition to have to satisfy the minister that every effort has been made to find someone in Canada interested enough to offer to manufacture the particular article.

I have no particular quarrel with the legislation as it deals with articles of a class or kind that are being made in Canada but I think we are going much too far and will handicap continuing technological development in Canadian industry if it is insisted that the government has a right to ask that evidence be produced indicating that no one in Canada is prepared or able to manufacture the particular article at an economic level and within a reasonable period of time. Therefore I should like to move an amendment at this time. While it is somewhat technical in that it changes the punctuation, its effect is to remove from clause 1, new section 2A, the whole of paragraph (b) of subsection 1 and the whole of paragraph (b) of subsection 3. Therefore I move:
That this Bill C-72, entitled "An act to amend the Customs Tariff", be amended by changing the semi-colon in clause (a) of subsection 1, section 1, to a period, and eliminating the immediately following word "and", and by removing the entire immediately following clause (b) and also in changing the comma in clause (a) of subsection 3 of said section 1 to a period, and eliminating the word "and" in this clause, and by eliminating entirely the whole of clause (b) of said subsection 3.
For purposes of clarification, may I repeat that if hon. members will look at the first page of Bill No. C-72 they will see that the amendment calls for the removal of the two paragraphs (b) on that page.

speechtext: I thank the minister for this information.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps I might say a word concerning the amendment moved by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If there is no comment about the regularity of the amendment I should like to put it first.

Mr. Chairman, I think the mover of the amendment, inasmuch as we have just received it, is obligated to explain in more detail what its effect is. I am sure he is prepared to do so for the benefit of the committee.

I made an effort to do so before but perhaps I can enlarge a little. It is my contention that the minister should not preside as a judge on a number of indefinite matters that are referred to in the bill. Let us assume that I operate an enterprise and I want to buy an additional piece of machinery. Under the terms of the bill, if that class or kind of machinery, or approximately the same class or kind, is not being manufactured in Canada I have the right to import it at a reduced rate of tariff. However, if it is a made-to-specification piece of machinery then under the terms of the bill I have to satisfy the minister first that it cannot be manufactured in Canada. I believe this is an imposition on Canadian industry.
I do not think the minister would want to be in the position of having to explore all over Canada the possibilities of whether or not somebody might be prepared to undertake the manufacture of this custom made article. I believe this is a handicap to expansion and efficiency in Canadian industrial production. In my opinion great delay might be involved which could mean considerable expense to Canadian enterprises. Who is to decide what is a reasonable period of time? I also believe the present provision could lead to misuse. Someone operating a little machine shop employing three or four men and who possibly was politically influential could claim that he was able to manufacture the article in question and he would keep running to the minister to use his influence to ensure that the order was given to him.
I feel that a new principle is being introduced into the Customs Tariff and that we would be much wiser if we left it out entirely. As I said before, I can see merit in an increase in tariffs on imported goods if such goods are actually being manufactured in Canada. However, to increase the tariff or to potentially increase the tariff because there may be someone who may decide that he wants to manufacture a certain article, within a

Customs Tariff
reasonable period of time, is going too far and will hurt Canadian industry much more than it will help it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The purport of this amendment should be clearly understood. The scheme of the bill, the bulk of which is contained in clause 1 now under debate, is to divide goods into two classes. The first class is shelf goods and the second is goods custom made according to specifications. The criteria laid down in the bill to assist in the determination of whether particular goods are of a class or kind made in Canada are different in the two cases because there is such a difference in the nature of the goods themselves.
This amendment would have the effect of eliminating from the provisions of the bill what is now provided in relation to that one class, namely goods custom made according to specifications. The amendment would confine the criteria in the bill entirely to shelf goods. I think that point should be clearly understood.
Now, the hon. member shows great solicitude for Canadian industry. He does not want them to be bothered gathering information or bringing forward knowledge in relation to whether or not the goods in question can be produced economically within a reasonable period of time. All I have to say is that Canadian industry is not making that kind of complaint or criticism. The expressions of Canadian industry have been to the effect that, at long last, some of the benefits they enjoyed in this regard up until what I have called the decade of erosion are going to be restored to them.
What is the great burden that is alleged by the hon. member to be laid upon Canadian industry? I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that Canadian industry will not be retarded technologically in this regard as the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam so erroneously concludes. The fact, which is apparent to all other hon. members of the committee, is that if this measure is adopted it will greatly assist the technological development of Canadian industry. It will give Canadians employment. It will certainly aid in developing productive Canadian enterprise.

The minister says this measure will aid Canadian employment. I hinted before that it is my conviction this is going to hinder Canadian employment and add to Canadian unemployment. The minister is attempting, by this paragraph (b), to impose a duty on goods that are not now being made in Canada. I believe this adds needlessly to the cost of production and eventually adds needlessly to consumer costs in Canada. Not only is the minister continuing to attempt

to raise a tariff wall against commodities imported into Canada that are being made in Canada now, but he is attempting to erect tariff barriers against articles that are not now being manufactured in Canada.
The effect of this measure will not be to cause Canadian factories to be built. If anything, this provision is going to hinder existing Canadian factories from improving there means of production. A lot of this machinery is very expensive machinery. There is a lot of money involved here. Some of the machinery is of a highly technical nature. I do not see Canadian industry becoming particularly involved in the manufacture of these goods. Even if they were, I think it is most unwise for the Canadian House of Commons to begin imposing tariff walls against goods, ostensibly for the protection of goods Canada hopes may some day be manufactured here.
Let us wait until the goods are being manufactured in Canada before we decide whether or not they need protection against imports. Let us not erect tariff barriers before the goods are actually being made.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The key words in the remarks just made by the hon. member are, "Let us wait". These words make a good summary of his approach to this matter. It does not matter that, in the meantime, Canadian producers have been deprived of what they possessed before under this legislation up until a decade ago. It does not matter that the jobs of Canadian workmen are involved. The hon. member says, "Let us wait". He says, let us wait, notwithstanding the fact that this legislation requires, before goods of this nature can be ruled to be of a class or kind made in Canada, that adequate facilities must exist in Canada for the economic production of such goods within a reasonable period of time. The hon. member says, do not pay any attention to the fact that the facilities are all here. It does not matter that Canadians can manufacture these goods on an economic basis within a reasonable period of time. So long as these specific goods, these identical goods, have not been manufactured yet in Canada, then there may not be any provision here for the assistance of the Canadian producer or Canadian workman.
This is just the sort of thing that has eroded the benefits of this legislation in the past. We are brought right back, by this stand, to the case of the power shovel. There had been a 2-yard shovel made in Canada and all the facilities existed in Canada for the manufacture of power shovels with a 24-yard capacity. However, because no shovels with a 2J-yard capacity had actually been manufactured up to that point, it was ruled then that a 2 4-yard shovel was of

a class or kind not made in Canada. This provision is intended to end the nonsense of that kind of interpretation. As long as the facilities exist in Canada for the production of such goods on an economic basis, not on some far fetched or fantastic basis but on an economic basis, and not at some far distant time in the future but within a reasonable period of time under all the circumstances having regard to the custom and usage of the trade in such cases, we say the goods should be ruled to be of a class or kind made in Canada. It is quite obvious that if they were of the kind being made now they would probably be shelf goods anyway. The provision which the hon. member wishes to strike out applies only in the case of goods that are made according to specifications.

There seems to be a good portion of the minister's remarks that is not relevant to the amendment and therefore tends to confuse the issue rather than clarify it. Frankly, I find it difficult enough to understand without any confusion being added. I do not believe the minister should be permitted to get away with what I consider to be a misrepresentation of the power shovel case.
The minister says, as a matter of fact, that facilities existed in Canada for the production of a 24-yard shovel, if I understood him correctly. The facts are that five years elapsed between the time that judgment was given and the time that the first 24-yard shovel was produced in Canada. The cost of providing the facilities to produce the 24-yard shovel-I have not the figure conveniently at hand-was a million dollars. These are the facts. I should not like anyone reading Hansard or the members of the committee to believe that facilities existed in Canada in that case because that is not in accordance with the findings of the tariff appeal board which dealt with this matter.
Perhaps we are now getting at the nub of why there is to be no appeal in these cases. The minister makes a finding of fact here by way of assertion that is very different from the finding of fact given by those who had the case before them and all the information surrounding it.

There is a special section dealing with appeals, as the chairman will know. I do not think I will speak on the matter of appeals at the moment, but I certainly will have something to say about it later on when we reach that subclause.

In introducing this bill on second reading yesterday the Minister of Finance, while he repeated some remarks he
Customs Tariff
had made on December 20 and in the subsequent debate that took place in the committee of ways and means on February 2, 3, 4, 15 and 27 and March 2, introduced a fair amount that was new. He did not in detail introduce the items that are referred to in Hansard of April 17th. I suggest that in large part, by throwing dust into their eyes, he was attempting to convince his mass of supporters in this house that they should support this kind of legislation.
One of the bases of our controversy here with regard to this legislation is whether or not this bill is restoring historic interpretation or whether or not we are going back to the interpretation that was acceptable to the Bennett administration of 1930. In this context I want to go back to an origin that is not the origin to which the Minister of Finance referred yesterday, namely 1873. I want to go back to the origin of a Conservative administration under Sir John A. Macdonald when the minister of finance was Mr. Foster. On that occasion he made clear the reason for the kind of tariff distinction about which we are concerned here. At what time Mr. Foster indicated that for the advancement of the manufacturing industry of this country it was important that they obtain at the lowest possible price the essential elements related to their business and these of course included machinery. I refer to the budget speech of 1890 when Hon. George E. Foster-and he was not a Liberal-said this as found in Hansard of that period. His remarks are to be found in the budget presentation at page 2550 of Hansard of March 27, 1890:
It is stated that the best and most improved machinery must be used by experimenters who put their money into enterprises the outcome of which they cannot certainly see. It is felt by them that the very best possible machinery should be got. It is felt by some that for a period at least there should be no restriction whatever on the buying of it, and by others, that there should be no other restriction than that imposed by the consideration whether or not the machinery is made in this country. Looking over the whole question, the government-
That is the government of that day, as long ago as 1890.
-have come to the conclusion that it will not be wise or prudent to resist this demand at the present time, in the interests of the development of that large part of the country's resources, and it is proposed-
That is in the budget of 1890.
-to allow mining machinery of a class and kind which is not made in Canada at the time of the importation-
That is essential. That is the difference between the legislation we have here now and the concept of "made in Canada" that has been traditional, not made in Canada at this time.

Customs Tariff
-to be imported into this country free for the period of three years and no longer.
That was the inception of this important element in the tariff structure that had a great deal to do with the impetus given to secondary industry to get going in Canada. On the amendment before us, Mr. Chairman, I am particularly concerned about statements that have been made by the Minister of Finance when he says that no rate change of tariff is involved in the legislation before us.
What I said, if the hon. member will be good enough to quote me accurately was that there is no change in any tariff rate created by this bill.
The Minister of Finance says to me at this moment that this legislation involves no change in rate with respect to tariff items.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I said it involves no change in the rate of any tariff item.

That is correct. I assert as I said yesterday, notwithstanding this technical sophistry of the Minister of Finance, that in its effect there will be increased costs to manufacturers in this country, to importers who want to compete on the basis of machinery they want to import, that are of import to the extent of thousands of dollars of excess taxes involved in the legislation that is here. The decision is going to be made by the minister and it is going to be made without appeal. I say that this is going to prejudice these manufacturing importers to a very great extent from here on.
In addition to that, we know that the Minister of Finance who has just interrupted has said that there is no change in the actual figures put in the Customs Tariff. There is not anybody who does business internationally through tariffs who does not know that there are two kinds of imposts with respect to tariffs. There is the rate that parliament has been given to decide upon in amendments to the Customs Tariff. But here is the big thing that divides a Liberal and a Conservative, namely the difference between administrative protection as administered in the department by the minister. If one will look at the recent tariff appeals, one will find that fairly regularly officials of the Department of National Revenue have been more protective in their outlook and in their decisions than has been the tariff board or the exchequer court or the supreme court in times when the tariff board, or the exchequer court or the supreme court had a chance to consider some of these matters that parliament had decided upon.
In other words, we have ministerial decision here. I suggest to the committee that

this is a serious matter, because it involves something more than the rates about which the minister talks. We are here dealing with an opportunity for ministerial discretion. This will enlarge that which is feared most by our exporters, our traders through GATT, our consumers and other people, namely, the invisible tariff.
The invisible tariff is the tariff created by bureaucrats, the tariff that is created by obstacles and road blocks, the kind of thing to which we object when we try to export to our principal customer, the United States. I say that this is clandestine protection. This is a matter that is sometimes more important than the technical definitions in the clauses of the Customs Tariff.
I said yesterday that Khrushchev might laugh when he sees these provisions. I did not add that I do not think the Minister of National Revenue wants to be a dictator. I have sat with him for a long time in this house. I do not think that is his desire.
I resented the fact that you called me single, when I have 14 grandchildren.

I really believe that the Minister of National Revenue wants to be a democrat. I have heard the minister speak in opposition. I thought he wanted the preservation of parliamentary rights. That is why I objected to the fact that the Minister of Finance boasted that, after long debate, not a word was changed in the bill that is now before us, from the wording contained in the resolutions proposed in the budget.
I do not think the Minister of National Revenue really wants these powers. I do not think he is that kind of man. When the government is going to change very shortly, I do not think he really wants to give those powers to his successors.

I say to the minister that I think the administration has been careless in the drafting of this power. Because they have behind them 204 supporters they have too much pride to back down and do something that is reasonable, just, and which should be done.
I am quite confident that on reflection of the debate at the resolution stage and at the stage of second reading the ministry is ashamed, having regard to what the leader of this ministry has said in times gone by as to the rights of a democratic parliament, that they have inserted this ministerial, autocratic right in this bill.

As I say I may have gone a little far yesterday in equating the Minister of National Revenue with Khrushchev, but I repeat-
I appreciate the compliment.
-that Khrushchev will perhaps have occasion to smile when he finds that in a democracy the Minister of National Revenue has these autocratic powers.

The house resumed from Tuesday, March 28, consideration in committee of Bill No. S-2, to incorporate Aurora Pipe Line Company-Mr. Woolliams-Mr. Flynn in the chair.
On clause 1-Incorporation.

Mr. Chairman, I am rather surprised by this bill being brought on for debate today. My recollection is that the hon. member for Bow River, who sponsored the bill, stated the last time this bill was debated that he was willing to answer any questions put by hon. members. I then posed three or four questions which he accepted and indicated he would forward to his principal and, in due course, present the answers to this committee. That hon. member is not here today and, therefore, cannot be blamed for not giving those answers for which I have asked. I feel the questions I asked are deserving of answers.
The questions were answered when you were not here.

We are now in committee and I will yield the floor to the hon. member if he can supply the answers. So far we have not received answers which would satisfy me at all except that which I feel is a reiteration of a lot of nonsense. When we expressed some concern in regard to the share structure of this company we were told to be quiet because we were not from Alberta. If the hon. member has something to contribute to this debate I will allow him to go ahead.
The hon. member for Vancouver-
South.

-South, presented some questions, to which the hon. member for Bow River said he would endeavour to obtain answers. On at least two occasions the hon. member for Winnipeg South placed on the record the answers to the questions which the hon. member for Vancouver South raised, but he was not here. That was all I wanted to point out. The hon. member may refer to my remarks in any way he likes and I could perhaps do the same but will allow him to continue now.

I thank the hon. gentleman. He is very kind. I have read every word of the debate on this bill but have not seen the answers to the questions which I asked. If the hon. gentleman will check the questions
[Mr. Speaker.)
I asked, as they appear in Hansard, he will perhaps then see that what he has now said is incorrect.
I cannot repeat in the same words the questions I asked but I suggest they have to do with the ownership of the parent company, Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company Limited, and specifically in regard to the percentage of stock held by the public which the committee was led to believe had been offered by the company to the Canadian public. That is just not correct. The rights to purchase shares were given to individual shareholders of the Continental Oil Company and the Hudson's Bay Company. I asked how many shareholders in Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company Limited were resident in Canada-not Canadian nationals-and how many shares these residents owned. I feel that is a rather easy question to answer because the records of the companies would show this. As far as I am aware this answer has not been given. That was one item in which I was interested. The other item I queried had to do with the supervisory personnel of the company.
I do not want to be accused of believing in a narrow nationalism or of being a person who is trying to throttle the development of this country but I would suggest that I have knowledge regarding this industry which is not matched by that of any other single member with the exception perhaps of the hon. member for Calgary South. I refer, of course, to the operation of that industry.
What do you want us to do, pat you on the back?
Have you a question?
You asked me to give you the answer.
If the hon. member has a question and will stand up in his place and ask it, instead of talking from his seat, I will be prepared to listen to him.
I am a friend of yours and will not challenge that boast.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

When I asked the questions in a previous debate I said I would not participate again in the debate at the committee stage. However, these questions have not been answered and I am not prepared to have the committee give approval to this bill until the answers are given. Quite frankly, as I have said before, because of the conditions set out by the sponsor and co-sponsor of the bill, I propose to vote against it. If a vote is called for and recorded on third reading I will vote against it then. I have said this before and now repeat it because the

sponsoring company has not taken into account the change in climate in this country regarding the development and use of our natural resources.
I welcome capital from the United States, Britain, Switzerland and every other country in the world but that capital must be used in partnership with Canadian capital. No matter what development takes place, if there are technically trained Canadians capable of holding the jobs, we do not have to bring in anyone to do the jobs in this country, with the exception, of course, of those individuals who have skills not possessed by men available here. What I am saying may sound like nonsense but I have been informed by Mr. Kerr, president of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited, with whom I spent an afternoon, that because of the present policy of developing Canadian understudies to executive personnel the company would be within the space of a year, 100 per cent managed by Canadians. He also informed me that the purchasing policy of that company had changed in that the company was giving preference to Canadian suppliers.
Are you referring to Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited?

Yes, and I was showing, by its present operation-not its previous operation under Mr. Tanner and Mr. Coates-what can be done. I happen to know that the Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company built a pipe line through the most difficult terrain in the world and that company from inception was 100 per cent Canadian.
I have been referring to a number of matters of national import, which override the sectional problems which exist in Alberta, and in respect of which I feel answers should be forthcoming. Natural resources, although under the control of the provinces, belong to the people of Canada as a whole and I feel that the development of these resources must take place having some regard to the Canadian people as a whole.
According to a news item in the Financial Post, Interprovincial Pipe Line is quite prepared to run a line down to Chicago to serve that area with condensates. There are alternative means of allowing this modest amount of 11,000 barrels of condensates per day to reach markets, but some in this house take the attitude "grab it all and fast, we might not have a chance tomorrow." Well, our resources are too valuable and-
Like the coal.

-too important to be bartered away in that fashion.
If the Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company had wanted to really show that they were 90205-6-238

trying to operate in a manner which was for the over-all good of this country, and for the over-all good of the company as well, they would have seen to it that part of the ownership of that company was vested in Canada through the stock market, through the offering of shares across Canada.
Do not tell me that Canadians are not willing to risk their money in ventures such as this. This is the old bogey that has been thrown around altogether too long. When the shares of Alberta Natural Gas came on the market brokers right across Canada said they would have to ration the shares. Likewise Alberta Gas Trunk Lines which is a model of financing and a model operation. Certainly they would not handle matters in the way that is proposed for this puppet company or for the parent company. This is the way these developments should be handled; this is the way the financing should be handled. It could be done and it has been done.
There is actually a dearth of opportunity for Canadian capital to invest in the development of Canadian resources. There are not enough places, not enough avenues for Canadian risk capital, and I am no capitalist. All my life I have worked for a salary. I will not be able to take advantage of any of these opportunities except perhaps in a most modest way, if at all. But as long as these developments are offered to the people of Canada, then we have a Canadian outlook in the operation of that company, and this is an outlook we cannot get in any other way. We cannot get it through lip service, by having half of the directors Canadian and the other half representing United States ownership, with a Canadian as chairman, because the control of the company is not in this country and perforce the directors will be simply rubber stamps for the directors of the parent company. In this instance the parent company happens to be Continental Oil Company because they have 67 per cent to 68 per cent of the shares of Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas, which in turn owns in its entirety Aurora Pipe Line.
I am not going to labour the points which have been pressed in this committee before with regard to capitalization stretching into millions to build half a mile of pipe line. The testimony in regard to this particular phase of the operation has been gone over in this committee time and time again. But it would be well for hon. members to read the testimony given to the standing committee and try to find out exactly what is being attempted. If they do I think there will be more of them come around to my way of thinking. The chief government whip has said that this is a private member's bill and hon.

members are free to vote for or against it as they so choose to do. This is true.
It may be that if this bill goes through the committee stage today-I doubt whether it will-there will still be a chance for the hon. member for Bow River to answer the questions I have placed before him. No statement has been made by the company, or I have seen no statement by any representative or any spokesman of the company, that they have any idea at all except that the operations of this company in this country can go on in the same manner and with some of the same philosophy that might have characterized a fruit company in one of the banana republics of Central America, or of more enlightened companies in Saudi Arabia, although in Saudi Arabia they are paying 75 per cent royalties and not 12J per cent.
The fundamental philosophy behind the opposition to this bill is simply that this company, which is gaining wealth through the exploitation of our natural resources, and which is rightly entitled to the profits it can make out of the enterprise, has a duty and a responsibility to the people of this country, a duty and a responsibility of which, as far as I can determine, it is not yet aware.

I have to take the responsibility for not answering the more significant questions of my hon. friend from Vancouver South as to the division of shareholders, the percentage of holdings in different countries. One reason is that he was not here at the time of the last debate on this bill in committee. On that occasion I answered his second question which has to do with Canadian participation. He will find that answer at page 3428 of Hansard of March 28, 1961, in the letter from management on the subject which I read into the record. I will not waste the time of the committee reading it again, because we have limited time in which to pass this bill through committee stage.
The answ'er to the first question as to the share participation and the division between individuals of different countries is set out in a letter from Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company to the legislative counsel, dated March 15, 1961. It reads in part as follows:

The letter goes on to say:
On completion of the initial distribution of the shares in 1957, the number of Canadian shareholders was 1,022 with total shareholdings of 306,287 shares and there has been a steady increase since that time to the totals shown above. During this same period the number of United States shareholders has declined by 747 and the total United States shareholdings by 278,337 shares.

Would the hon. member repeat the figures with regard to Canadian participation and particularly the percentage that Canadian participation represents compared with total public holdings of 9.64 per cent? I think the hon. member said 2.96 per cent but I am not sure.

The number of Canadian
shareholders is 1,410, the percentage of total shareholders is 11.80, the number of shares is 525,299, the percentage of public shareholdings is 30.72 and the percentage of total shares is 2.96. Therefore when you look at the column of figures you will see that actually the majority of shares publicly held are held in Canada and the United Kingdom.

I should like to make a few comments, Mr. Chairman. When the shares were first issued Canadian shareholders owned 306,000 whereas their shareholdings now have grown to 525,000. I think this reinforces my argument about the willingness of Canadians to invest in resource development because they have had to purchase these shares either in the United Kingdom

or the United States and most likely they have done so in the United States because holdings by people in that country have gone down.
The same story is given by the management of McIntyre gold mine who in their last statement pointed out that their shares had been almost 100 per cent repatriated. Whereas in previous years the majority had been owned in the United States, over 90 per cent are now owned in Canada.
The point is, however, that in the present instance, although Canadian participation has risen to 30.72 per cent of the total public ownership of shares, the total public ownership is only 9.64 per cent of all the shares of the company and Canadian ownership of shares in this company is something under 3 per cent. That does not strike me as being what one would call a reasonable Canadian participation, and I come back to the fact that Canadians have increased their holdings by 66 to 70 per cent over what they were originally in 1957 when these shares were first offered.
This company might well have considered taking some of their treasury stock and making it available across Canada in order to increase Canadian participation to some point where the company might be truly classed as Canadian. Less than 3 per cent does not make it a Canadian company and if it is going to prosper from the development of our resources I suggest it should become more of a Canadian company than it is now.

Mr. Chairman, this is the first opportunity I have taken to speak on the bill at any of its stages. The title intrigued me, of course, when I first saw it because in our part of the country we have had in the past a rather small but clamorous group interested in secession from the province of Ontario and the setting up of a new province which was labelled Aurora by one of the more imaginative in the group. I have often thought that their scheme was highly imaginative, perhaps too imaginative, and therefore when this measure came before the house I was interested in hearing that some of my colleagues found it imaginative.
Quite frankly, I have enjoyed some of the debates that have taken place on the bill, no more so than the contribution I have heard today by the hon. member for Vancouver South. A number of members of parliament at the various stages of the discussion of the bill in the house and in the standing committee have gone to great lengths to disclaim their own knowledge of what is involved in this matter. When the hon. member for Winnipeg South introduced the bill he made it very clear that he was speaking strictly on the basis of information that had 90205-6-2384

been given to him and was not setting himself up as any kind of authority. There were many challenges flying back and forth across the house on second reading in that regard, and on the part of those who were very anxious to get the bill through the argument seemed to be that we did not need to know anything about it anyway, that it was merely a matter of incorporating the company. Therefore they said that we should pass the bill because the place where members could really find out things was in the standing committee on railways, canals and telegaph lines.
Then there were even some who felt that committee really did not matter too much because the matter would finally have to go before the national energy board and they would really look after our interests and the interests of all Canadians. Then, of course, there were those songbirds from Alberta who told us about the sweet things that happen during the Alberta conservation board hearings. We were all going to be protected, therefore, by these other agencies in any decision we might make to push this bill through on second reading or in the committee.
1 should like now, Mr. Chairman, to raise a matter on which I hope you will let me continue for a minute or two before you decide whether or not I am out of order. I believe it is relevant to this bill. I believe the treatment this bill received in the committee-I am not saying this by way of criticism of the members of that committee- is a fine indication it is about time we equipped ourselves with the resources for getting more of the information we need through the establishment of a permanent research group attached to the standing committees of this house. In reading the report of the committee one finds that hon. members of good will such as the hon. member for York North and the hon. member for Calgary South, whose opinions I respect, came forward and expressed some views. The final analysis was that the bill was sort of shoved through because we did not really know the answers to the questions that were asked. I can only assume from reading the report of the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines for Tuesday, March 21, that the house committee was really not able to assist in solving the problem from the point of view that the hon. member for Vancouver South and the hon. member for Vancouver East were prepared to present.
This situation indicates to me that it is time we gave our standing committees the personnel they need to enable us to know that when we go into a committee we are not completely helpless in facing parliamentary agents or representatives of these companies.

Private Bills
I will not say any more on this subject now. However, I feel that a great deal of the discussion that has taken place could have been prevented if we could have been sure, both in the committee and in the house, that we could have obtained the details we needed instead of obtaining information in dribs and drabs accompanied by a great deal of invective back and forth.
Oh, fiddlesticks; you are just delaying the bill.

I hear an interruption from the hon. member for Acadia. I am glad to have this interruption because I know he represents a definite point of view. It seems to me that in the province of Alberta they have some kind of fossil deposits. They have discovered ancient animals. It is known that that part of the province contains some of the oldest remains in existence. In taking the position that he has, and I say this quite honestly, it seems to me that the hon. member for Acadia is representing one of the oldest positions in Canadian and North American politics and to me it is a fossil position.
I have strayed away from the point-
Would the hon. member permit a question?
I am always ready to permit a question.

The hon. member has gone to great lengths to describe the research group the committee should have. I am sure there is no one more qualified to speak about committee work than the hon. member, and he has done a lot of research in connection with committee work. However, can the hon. member tell me why the hon. member for Vancouver East and others did not ask the same questions in the committee when the parties were there to answer them that they have been asking in the house?

I could not answer a question concerning what role our members played. Normally, I am a member of this committee but I was bumped off the committee because the bill seemed to affect the regions of other hon. members. I do know that I found the committee's reports interesting. As a matter of fact, the central reason for my speech today is the information contained in the latter that the hon. member for Vancouver East received from the Pembina company and filed with the committee. When I compare the information contained in the letter with the information that has been given to us by the hon. member for Bow River and the hon. member for Winnipeg South, I am convinced that the hon. member for Vancouver South has an excellent point. I had not realized

that a pipe line company in Canada today was so truly Canadian as this organization seems to be.

I am sure the hon. member would permit another question. Did he not see in the committee proceedings a statement to the effect that if Interprovincial Pipe Lines, I think it is, or the Pembina people, were given the contract by the United States oil company, then the United States oil company would be granted controlling interest in the Canadian firm? I am sure this statement appears in the evidence, and the hon. member would not want the members of this committee to be led astray.

I had assumed from the fact they were being given the controlling interest that it was a matter of trade. I want to come closer to the hon. member who has been interrupting me. I want to say that I have never been able to feel money has any flag on it. It does not seem to me that you can really put a flag on capital, especially in North America. It always seems unreasonable to me, especially in view of the part of the country I represent, to get so worked up over the question of the source of capital. We have had to face this problem since Canada first came into being, and the United States faced it before we did.
On the other hand, in recent years we have developed an attitude, which some people credit to the present government, that the principle of Canadian ownership in any further development of resource fields will be the No. 1 principle. It seems to me this subject was debated when the national energy board was created. The Prime Minister has included this topic in some of those lovely little television performances I have observed a number of times. I seemed to feel that I and all the other little Canadians were going to enjoy a chance to get into the development of natural resources.
I talked to a member of the national energy board the other day for whom I have a great deal of respect. I am not going to go into detail about what he said, but he certainly indicated to me he did not have any particular concern arising from what he knew about this particular line. I could be assured, he said, that the national energy board would give the full benefit of all their resources to any hearing on this matter and that they would also take a look at the opinions expressed by the members of parliament. This is fine.
However, if I may return to the point I would say that a principle has been presented, first by the hon. member for Vancouver East but possibly more forcibly by the hon. member for Vancouver South. In the light of this particular principle, I do not see how we can

agree to the passage of this bill. It seems to me it is a poor bill in the sense that it is the wrong kind of company bringing it forward. I make these remarks on the question of principle.
However, I should like to turn to a couple of other aspects of the bill that intrigue me. I really have not got a clear picture from anything put forward by the dual sponsors, but it seems to me that the question that was bothering the hon. member for York North was whether or not the launching of this particular organization would cripple, damage, ruin or cause trouble for the Pembina people, the Foothills people, in their attempt to get a much larger share of the product to market. The hon. member for York North was good enough to reveal that he did have a financial interest in the company involved. I think we all respect his integrity, though our views may differ from his. I do not believe the answers we have had from the two sponsors really clear this up. Reference has been made to the fact that this subject is too technical for us and we should therefore let the national energy board deal with it. It seems to me that it is in principle at least a fairly simple matter.
We have a company that has been working for two years part of the time in co-operation with the sponsors of this bill, and they naturally feel that the invasion in the field by the incorporation of this company might cause them difficulty in their attempts to set up the matter. This is the company-this company related to Pembina-that has shown to us that it has a magnificent ratio of Canadian ownership and of Canadian employees, one with which this other company cannot compare at all.
In this regard I should just like to point out that the Pembina Pipe Lines Limited company stresses that all its permanent employees are Canadians. This information was not contradicted before the committee. As a matter of fact, Mr. Burgis, I think that is his name, agreed that the general information contained in it seemed to go along with what had been filed, I imagine under oath before what has been made much of, namely a court of record before the Alberta group. I am therefore left with the feeling that, on a Canadian principle put forward by a number of members very feelingly, the bill is unsatisfactory. But from the point of view of the possibility of this company "snafuing" the works for the company that is already in the field, I have grave doubts that have not been answered.
There are a number of questions that I should like to put to the sponsor of the bill. One of the arguments that he put forward is that in 1957 public shares were offered
Private Bills
on the market to Canadians. I observe the hon. member for Vancouver South shaking his head with regard to the point to which I was referring. I was wrong. It is just that the shares of the company were listed on the Toronto stock exchange in 1957 and since that time have been actively traded and have been available for purchase by any Canadian who wished to invest in them. But as the hon. member for Winnipeg South has indicated in his statement, the shares available to the public and traded on the Toronto stock exchange are a pittance in relation to the total shares that exist in the company.
Despite the fact that in the letter he put on record at page 3428 of Hansard in which Mr. Burgis said that the company does not have any need for additional equity capital at the present time, I should very much like to know from him whether it might not be the time, in view of the criticisms that have been made, for these two organizations, namely Hudson's Bay and Continental, to make available to the public more of these holdings they now have. It seems to me that this would be an answer. I should like more of an explanation than we are given in this letter filed by the hon. member for Winnipeg South.
There is another point about which I should like to hear from the sponsors of the bill and it is this. I know I could get this information on my own, but I feel they should provide it. As found at page 3429 of Hansard, we are told that the company has issued and sold to Canadian investors three different issues which in total amount to $28,600,000. I should like to know more about the circumstances in connection with this debt issue. I should like to know whether they were debentures that were issued along with any shares at various times. I should like to know whether this debt issue is held completely by Canadians, or just how the matter came along. It would seem to me remarkable if this company has never, since it got operating here, put on the Canadian market an issue of shares and yet at the same time has offered debentures to the Canadian public. It would appear to me that it has been taking advantage of all the savings that might exist in various markets in Canada. I should like to think that if they could raise this much money on debt issues, they could also find all kinds of purchasers for stock put on the market. I know that the value of shares at the present time, or the median value of shares say for the last year, might indicate whether or not this is a sensible request for information.
In connection with this bill, I have been greatly interested to discover that the two Calgary papers take different points of view

Private Bills
on it. I was very much reassured when accusations were ringing in this house that a filibuster was going on. I wondered about the position of the members of this particular party. I wondered whether we were completely off on the wrong track. I therefore went to the trouble of checking in publications in Alberta and in other parts of the country. I was pleased to discover that the position that has been advanced here and has been supported so well by the hon. member of Vancouver East and by the hon. member of Vancouver South, has been supported by three publications, including the Calgary Herald. Even in the Calgary Albertan which rips strips off the C.C.F. for deliberately in a sense abusing parliament, it is conceded that the factor that the company would be United States controlled is something to which this House of Commons should give serious consideration. I was interested to discover that the periodical Saturday Night had an expression of opinion that would seem to indicate that the stand made against this bill has a great deal of merit.
By saying this I am not suggesting that this kind of support or this kind of view of whatever actions we or any other party may take is an essential thing. However, it is somewhat satisfying to find this situation in view of the bitter invective that has been hurled at the members of this party and even at the hon. member for Vancouver South when he has been making his objections to this bill.
It seems to me that the sponsor-I refer especially to the hon. member for Bow River *-has been far too aggressive, especially for a sponsor, in making this kind of approach. As I conclude, I can only add to that criticism that it seems to me most regrettable that he has not been here more often to present the case in a calmer and quieter way that may have led us to take a different attitude.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
The charge has been made that the aggressiveness was not shown in the committee. Hon. members will know that I am not a member of the committee. However, I availed myself of the opportunity of attending the committee hearings and listening to the arguments that were put forward. I believe that the hon. member who raised this problem a few moments ago will agree with me that the discussions that took place in the committee may have certainly been augmented to a great degree by the bits of information that have been continually fed to the house by the sponsors of the bill.
The hon. member for Vancouver East is specifically interested in the financial arrangement as it affects another company that has already been given the opportunity of doing a similar type of development work and the

hon. member for Vancouver South is interested in it from the point of view of the Canadian content. Both these hon. gentlemen in particular have been answered at great length and the answers that have been given have been supplemented and have been much more extensive than was the information that was given to the committee in the first place.
Many of the hon. members who sat in that committee were interested in one aspect of the bill and were not particularly interested in the over-all bill in relationship to the viewpoint of the two hon. members I have mentioned. Those hon. members, were more concerned with the financial arrangements than were some others. The information now available to the committee is a great deal more extensive than that available in the committee hearing and we are now more able to make a decision.
I am interested in this matter from another point of view. This is not completely divorced from the point of view expressed today by the hon. member for Vancouver South. I am interested in the relationship which this particular industry, or this particular company *-because it is almost all of the industry and will be the key to the industry-will have on Canadian development and the development of Canadian secondary industry in western Canada.
I spoke to someone the other day-the hon. member for Acadia may laugh-who pointed out that this was like putting a tap on the bottom of the oil barrel in western Canada, running this half mile of tap over to the United States and dumping the whole thing there.

Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member permit a correction? He keeps on pronouncing my constituency as "Arcadia". There is no "r" in the spelling of my constituency. Also, it is in Alberta, not Nova Scotia, as the hon. member probably thinks.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I thank the hon. member for his correction. I can assure him that I did not think he came from the maritimes area of Arcadia. I am familiar with the fact that he comes from western Canada and I will try to pronounce his constituency correctly in future.
If this is the tap on the bottom of the oil reserves, it seems to me that consideration of this matter should be extensive because we are discussing a resource that can be as advantageous to Canadian secondary development as the oil industry has been to those areas in the United States which are going to benefit from these oil reserves.
The development that has taken place around these refinery centres in the United

States has been phenomenal. It has been accomplished in a very short period of time, and the results of this development have brought untold wealth and benefits to the areas serviced by secondary development in the oil industry.
It is our hope that parliament will give consideration to this matter in relation to this particular bill. It is not enough to say that we should leave it to the Alberta oil and gas conservation board or the national energy board to make the decision. I think it is obvious that the obligation is on parliament to make the decision, and we should do something about it.
As we look around our country and the world today we see that there is a growing desire on the part of the people to keep their countries for themselves. We are witnessing a war in Cuba today, or a counter-revolution to overthrow the government that has as its motto "Cuba for the Cubans". That motto is similar to that the Conservative party adopted in the last election, "Canada for the Canadians".
I think those of us who do not support the Conservative party have an obligation to make sure that hon. members do not forget that particular fact. We have an obligation to see that they live up to the slogan "Canada for the Canadians".
I do not object to United States capital coming into the country. I do not think it is necessary that all the money going into this development should be Canadian, but I do think we should use our resources to the best of our ability. If we are going to drain our natural resources we are not going to develop any type of secondary industry in our country.
The Canadian chamber of commerce, which supports the present government, have this to say in their publication "Policy Declarations":
The chamber also urges its members to promote and support federal and provincial and business policies which will lead (1) to properly integrated development of Canada's natural resources in the interests of the nation as a whole; (2) to government policies in resources management that will ensure maintenance and where possible expansion of all renewable resources; (3) to fiscal and taxation policies consistent with good resource management and (4) to the development of educational programs with respect to the conservation and efficient utilization of natural resources.
They go on to talk about off shore drilling, and so on.
You are talking nonsense.
