Mr. Chairman, I was unable at five o'clock to make certain remarks in regard to the amendment put forward at that time, and because the amendment has been dealt with since I will not attempt to do so now. My proposed remarks will have to remain off the record of Hansard. Perhaps many hon. members in committee would be better off if their remarks were left out. I would suggest, however, that there is a problem in regard to the discussion of this bill because one clause essentially contains the whole substance of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There are three other clauses on the next page.

Yes, but there is only one main clause. It is subdivided in such a way that it becomes somewhat inconvenient for discussion. Perhaps in dealing with the subject matter of clause 1 it would be as well to raise one point at a time, and I propose to limit my remarks at this stage to one particular point. Perhaps I can do this best by indicating at the outset of my remarks the amendment I propose to move at a later stage. The substance of that proposed amendment, which I will move at the conclusion of my remarks, is that the clause be amended by striking out subsection 3 of section 2A.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Did you say subsection 3 of section 2A?

Customs Tariff
Actually this refers to the whole section.
Over-all, the hike is 15 per cent.

Yes, the difference resulting from the decision in most cases increases the duty by about 15 per cent. If the decision goes against the importer, even if it is a fair decision, it is an increase of the taxation; for it is 7J per cent when it is not made in Canada and 22J per cent when it is made in Canada. It is an increase of 200 per cent in the taxation rate applicable because of a decision made by the minister, which is not subject to appeal. Surely the principle should be that taxation should be set by this parliament. It is no answer to say that the rates of duty on the different items are set by parliament if the minister can, without being subject to any appeal or giving the citizen any right of application to the tariff board or to the courts, decide which rate is applicable. Surely this is something the minister will need to explain more fully than he has done heretofore in the debate.
I do not suggest that the minister will abuse this wilfully of his own volition, but surely he should not be left in a position whereby on his own whim or caprice he can raise the taxation as between two importers of the same article by that kind of percentage or that kind of interpretation. Surely that is not what our system contemplates at all, and surely a minister of the crown ought not to 90205-6-239
Customs Tariff
be left in the position where it can be said of him in any particular case that he did that.
It would be possible to elaborate upon the reasons why the right of appeal should be left in and not taken away, and why the right of taxation should be left in the hands of parliament and not given to the minister, as this clause in effect does. One could elaborate on that and bring in all those loud-sounding speeches that were delivered by the Prime Minister and others of his supporters on the bill of rights about the rights of the citizen to not be removed other than by due process of law, but perhaps at the committee stage it is not necessary to go into that. Surely in the light of the clause that is now before the committee, those words were a mockery. Therefore, without further ado, Mr. Chairman, I would move, seconded by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate:
That subsection 3 of section 2A be struck out.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the amendment carry?

Mr. Chairman, I should like to start by echoing the words which have been uttered by the hon. member for Ottawa West about the loud-sounding speeches made and the hollow arguments used in this debate so far. Certainly no better description could be given of the speeches made by members of the opposition. Because of the fact that my colleague, the Minister of Finance, refrained from replying in the debate on second reading and I have not spoken at all and also the fact that we have now spent eight days on this debate, I would hope that by temperate statement and restraining oneself from saying the things that one would like to say we might be able to come to a decision on this matter without further prolonged and unnecessarily prolix discussion. I will not say "stupid" although one might be tempted to do so.
That is a very good way of getting legislation through.

It is clearly in keeping with what we have had to put up with for eight days but I am trying to restrain myself. I know it is not true of the hon. member for Ottawa West and the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River who do have some knowledge of this subject, but one would almost think, in view of the debate that has taken place so far, that we were dealing with a new subject entirely of which hon. members opposite had no knowledge whatsoever. There is nothing new about this matter at all.
One would think that a "made in Canada" ruling was something which had suddenly developed or was being proposed in this legislation for the first time. As a matter of

Customs Tariff
fact, "made in Canada" rulings have been in force in Canada under various terminology, as the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate pointed out, for probably over half a century.
We have been discussing appeals. It might be interesting to point out this fact in passing over these things, and I hope, as I say, that we will pass over them fairly quickly and temperately. Sometimes one hears the late R. B. Bennett referred to in caustic terms as a protagonist of high tariffs. It might be interesting to point out to the committee in passing that the right of appeal to the tariff board was brought into effect by the late R. B. Bennett.
But his staff had the final say.

During the years from 1921 to 1930, however, when another government was in power, with the exception of a short period in 1925 and 1926, there was a right of appeal to the customs board which was comprised of the deputy minister of customs, the assistant deputy minister of customs, another officer appointed by the deputy minister of customs, the deputy minister of excise and the deputy minister of taxation. That certainly could not be said to be an impartial board to pass upon appeals, and it was the late Hon. R. B. Bennett who created the tariff board and provided for appeals to that board, to which subject we have referred from time to time during this debate.
As I have said, there is nothing new about "made in Canada" rulings. They have been made over a long period of time. During my short term as Minister of National Revenue I have made scores of "made in Canada" rulings. Sometimes three or four a week come up, sometimes three or four a month. As a matter of fact, I made four last week under the provisions of the statute as it has existed for many years. So there is nothing particularly new about this.
All the bill does is (a) to insert the word "approximately" in order, as the Minister of Finance has pointed out, to restore the ambit of the act as it was intended and as it operated up to ten years ago and (b) to provide for a class of goods which has not heretofore been made but with respect to which the capability to make them exists, and so on and so forth. These are the purposes plus the fact that within a very narrow compass, to which I will refer in a moment, the right of appeal has been limited and in a very technical sense restricted. That is the only difference between the bill now before the committee and the act on the statute books today under which

the Minister of National Revenue has operated up till this moment.
There has been a great deal said about doing away with the right of appeal. There has been a great deal said about transgressing upon the rights of parliament, that parliament is the only body that should pass upon tariffs and that the bill before us constitutes an abrogation of the right of appeal and a reflection upon the rights of parliament. As I said, Mr. Chairman, one could refer to that argument in language which probably would prolong the debate for a much greater length of time than I should like to see it prolonged. However, pursuant to an order of the house moved by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River the decisions and orders which the Minister of National Revenue has made under section 38 of the Customs Act since December 1, 1958, were tabled in the house today. Section 38 of the Customs Act as it has applied going back to December 1, 1958, has nothing to do with the bill before us tonight.
May I ask the minister a question?
I should like to keep the floor if I may until I finish.
Would he allow me to ask a question later?
I surely will. I gave this document to the Clerk this afternoon for tabling in the House of Commons.

After seven days of
debate.

There are, I believe, 44 different rulings which have been made by the Minister of National Revenue under section 38 of the Customs Act since December 1, 1958. This act has been on the statute books for many years. It was in force under the regime of the preceding government, and with various and slight modifications-
This is a new ruling.
These are not new rulings. These are rulings which have been made under section 38 of the Customs Act which has been in force in Canada for at least a quarter of a century.
It was not section 38 before.

Without taking the time of the committee, I will simply suggest that those who are worried about the effect of making these rulings, and I know there are some who are worried, should peruse the document which was tabled in the House of Commons today. Section 38 authorizes the Minister of

National Revenue to fix values for duty without consultation with parliament. The minister has the right under that section to fix the value for duty purposes. I am not going to bore the committee because I do not wish to take too much time. I have marked 20 or 30 different orders which have been made and which are not subject to appeal.
These are ministerial rulings made by the minister pursuant to the act and whether they are right or wrong, and I hope they are right, they are not subject to appeal. So when we hear the talk we have heard about trespassing upon the right of appeal I suggest that one should look at the return which was tabled today and then decide how much substance there is to this argument about infringement of the right of appeal. There are orders here wherein the Minister of National Revenue has said that there shall be cost plus an advance of 25 per cent. There are other orders in which the Minister of National Revenue has ordered that there shall be cost plus an advance of 50 per cent. There have been orders dealing with imported goods from foreign countries where we have said that the value of the goods from that country shall be equal to the cost of the goods from another country.
As an example, I may cite the case of Chinese paint brushes. This is a very minor case, but it is one in which we have said that the value for duty shall be the value of the brushes exported from Great Britain rather than from China. One could go on and on giving examples. I would hope that hon. members who are concerned about this matter would take advantage of the opportunity to read the return which was filed today showing the powers which have been vested in the minister of national revenue, not by this proposed amendment, but which have been vested in the minister for over half a century by the parliament of Canada. This amendment relates to a minor matter. I would suggest, too, that these powers have been exercised, not by minions as was suggested yesterday, but by senior officials of the Department of National Revenue. These are men of experience who have been trained and who have spent a lifetime in the service of the department.
Although I appreciate the statement made by the hon. member for Ottawa West a while ago to the effect that no minister could possibly have the time to deal with all these matters, I want to assure the committee through you, Mr. Chairman, that there has not been an order made concerning a "made in Canada" ruling or fixing the value for duty which the minister has not perused personally, checked and rechecked before he signed it. There have been, I may say, scores and 90205-6-239i
Customs Tariff
scores of such orders. If the committee, in its wisdom, sees fit to pass these amendments, as I hope it will, I can assure you that these rulings and orders will be made in a manner no different from that of the past. I am sure that my predecessor the late Dr. McCann and his predecessor the Right Hon. J. L. Ilsley never made these rulings except in consultation with the senior officials who have available to them all the memoranda on the previous rulings, documents which go back almost to confederation and certainly for 60 or 70 years.
The Minister of National Revenue, with the advantage of these documents and the advantage of the experience and advice of the senior officials, has to make the decisions which he makes pursuant to the various sections of the act. As my hon. friend reminds me, there is no appeal from the decisions here. I invite hon. members to look at these orders tomorrow. They will see decisions here in which the value for duty was increased 100 per cent over what was alleged to be the fair market value. There are others in which the value for duty has been increased 25 per cent, 50 per cent and others where it has been marked up specifically by $5 or 50 cents, whatever the case may be. There are 44 of them, and they have been made since December 1, 1958. Every one of the rulings was made by the individual who happened, for the moment, to be the minister of national revenue. They were made without the right of appeal.
Then, we hear talk for seven days about the fact that we are transgressing upon the rights of parliament; that we are depriving someone of the right to appeal. Is it any wonder that one could speak of this matter in a way which would, I am afraid, prolong this debate to a much greater length than I hope it will last. I have been referring to one section, section 38 of the Customs Act, but I have in my hand a list of 64 different sections of the Customs Act, the Customs Tariff Act and the Excise Act under which the decisions of the minister of national revenue are final and without appeal.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: How many different sections?

Sixty four, and of those 64 different sections, 62 of them were on the statute books of this country when the present government took office in 1957. There are two of them which were enacted by the present government, the one fixing the value plus a reasonable mark-up for profit, and the one fixing the values of fruit to be imported. Not one order has been made under either section.

Customs Tariff
I think possibly some weeks ago I misled the committee when I said no action had been taken under the revisions of the Customs Act in 1958. There have been many decisions to which I have just referred which have been made under the revisions of the Customs Act in 1958. However, the revisions of the Customs Act were all consolidations of existing sections with the exception of the two amendments to which I have referred and under those two amendments no orders have been made. I do not believe I should worry the committee by enumerating these various sections. I have marked a lot of them and if I had the time I believe I would have a reasonable degree of fun by enumerating some of the powers given, rightly or wrongly, to the minister of national revenue and which have been exercised for almost half a century. They have been exercised by my predecessors and, at the moment, they are exercised by me as minister. They will be exercised by other ministers who come after us. In not one single case, Mr. Chairman, is there a right of appeal from the decision of the minister. Rightly or wrongly, the decision of the minister is final.
Then, it has been suggested that these minor little amendments which we are making today are an infringement of the rights of parliament; that they transgress upon the courts or obliterate the courts. As I have said, the language in which I should like to describe this argument is such as I should like to refrain from using at the moment. I have these four typewritten pages which set forth the sections of various acts to which I have referred. On the last page I notice one section which says that the minister's decision shall be final and he shall be the sole judge as to whether printed material is educational or otherwise. Well, that is not too heavy a responsibility but nevertheless it is indicative of the powers which are given to the minister of national revenue.
I have given some of the background of the practice which has prevailed throughout all these years as a result of the authority given by parliament. We are now dealing with amendments which, to some extent, enlarge the power of the minister with respect to goods which are ordered by specification and goods which are approximately of a class or kind. My colleague the Minister of Finance has dealt at some length with these matters and I do not propose at this time to weary the committee by dealing with those matters further. There are several powers of appeal given, but the decision of the minister shall be final with respect to the normal Canadian consumption of the goods described. My good, 
personal friend the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate said last night he could not understand why this appeal was to the "consumption", and why it was not to the "production" of the goods made in Canada.
I did not advocate that.

But yet my hon. friend and, I think, various other hon. members argue that the minister can fix normal consumption, that the minister can fix the figure very low, that he can have his friends and give them a hand-out. There was a score of quotations such as that emanating from the mouth of my friend the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. Yet in the same breath last night he said that he could not understand why the appeal was from consumption and not from production.
Mr. Chairman, I think the hon. gentleman does not want to misinterpret what I said last night.
Not at all.

I said that I opposed the abolition of any kind of appeal. However, I said that if one were seeking to make a case for refusing an appeal, I could see slightly more sense in the case of production in Canada than I could in the case of consumption in Canada. I said that because I thought the producers might want to keep their production secret but I could not see why anyone would be interested in keeping the consumption secret. However, I want it completely understood that I am opposed to any abrogation of any existing right of appeal.

Abrogation of any right of appeal as suggested in this legislation is infinitesimal as compared with the abrogations of rights of appeal which occurred under legislation enacted when my hon. friend was in the privy council and in the privy closet for years preceding me. It is rather refreshing to hear that this wandering gentleman from Winnipeg who sat in the closet here for 11 years and now has arrived fresh and salty from Bonavista-Twillingate, should be suspicious of the activities of the government in this country. It must suggest to hon. gentlemen that the companions and the associations which he had during those years rather twisted his thoughts and suggested to him suspicions.
Why do you not talk about the bill that is before the committee?

These suspicions certainly would never occur to any of us on this side of the house. What I am getting at is this. If my hon. friends' suspicions are correct

and if the minister of national revenue can arrange for a coterie of friends somewhere in a room or, as he said, in a closet, to look after them, why have an appeal from the decision of the minister with respect to Canadian production, because it is Canadian production that is going to be made by those friends. But there is an appeal from Canadian production, from the activities of the minister's friends, from the activities of anybody who might be associated with this government within Canada. The appeal lies in Canadian consumption. Everyone knows that Canadian consumption-and my hon. friend will well realize this-consists of Canadian production plus imports less Canadian exports.
One question why there should be no appeal on that matter of consumption, I can give one little illustration of a case which was before my department and the tariff board in the end last year and the year previous. It was the so-called "ball bearing" case. As I pointed out on an earlier occasion, and I do not want to trespass on the time of the committee now, the Department of National Revenue, because of its dealings with all of these producers and the importers, the confidential nature of our transactions and all the documents involved, is in the position-and it is the only one-of getting all the information-and we did not always get it all-which is necessary on the case. In the ball bearing case it was necessary for the Department of National Revenue to get the information with respect to ball bearings produced outside of Canada. What did we find? After consulting with the United States embassy and checking the sources of information there we found there were 18 suppliers in the United States manufacturing ball bearings with which we were concerned. We found there were 94 of them producing ball bearings in Europe. We found a large number-we were never quite certain how large the number was, I may say frankly- producing ball bearings in Japan and others possibly in Hong Kong. For months and months the department checked and rechecked through the embassies, through our own commercial counsellors and through every source of information available, trying to find out the number of ball bearings produced and brought into this country.
Added to that, of course, was our own production which could be very easily determined. In the end after seven months, we were faced with the necessity of making a decision and we made one. We fixed the consumption of ball bearings in Canada. It took us seven months to get this information. There was the possibility of an error but there was a much greater necessity for giving
Customs Tariff
a definite ruling and for making it final so that business would know where it fitted and whether it could go ahead or whether it could not do so.
If after having spent months and months in trying to get this information and having used every possible source of information which is available to the department with all its far flung sources of information, some interested person could enter an appeal to the tariff board on some figment of imagination that there might have been a mathematical error in the computation of this consumption, then the situation would have been delayed for another two years before a definite decision could be made. How could business be carried on in that particular field?

So Queen Elizabeth is
wrong?

I am not sure about Queen Elizabeth but I know that my hon. friend for Kenora-Rainy River is wrong. But that is the reason why we have said that, in so far as Canadian consumption is concerned, it is necessary in the end, having exhausted every possible avenue open to us in order to get it certain. In order to give a decision, in order that business may map its course and know where it is going we say that the decision of the minister in this mathematical computation in this area shall be final and shall not be subject to appeal. I ask you, Mr. Chairman, to compare that section with those to which I referred a moment ago in which, on important matters, no appeal has been allowed since the Customs Act was enacted.
Then there are two other areas in which there is no appeal and in which the decision of the minister shall be final. Section 1 is where goods are custom made to specification.
Whose specification?

Surely any person with reasonable intelligence and having access to the documents can determine whether goods are being ordered by some hon. gentlemen opposite from a manufacturer according to the specifications of the hon. gentleman opposite or any hon. gentleman, and the person ordering them according to specification and not according to standard production of the manufacturer. Surely there is nothing there which causes any concern. It is a simple little elementary question of fact.
Why take two years to decide?
My hon. friend the Leader of the Opposition says it might take two years to decide.

That is what you said.

Customs Tariff
The minister said so. That is what he said a moment ago.

I said that a capricious person or a person wanting to enter a capricious appeal might take two years, and since they raised this matter, Mr. Chairman, I will deal with it. We have had many motives imputed here. It has been suggested that there are friends with whom one might consort, that somebody must be getting a pay-off. The only reason I can see for this exaggerated or prolonged debate is the fact that there must be somebody, some period of someone on the other side of the chamber who is afraid of the rulings that may be made and he wants to be able to maintain a system of superficial and artificial appeal so that he can avoid rulings for a period of two, three or four years. One argument is just as good as the other as far as that is concerned.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt the minister but I must inform him that his time has expired.
Let him go on.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is the committee agreeable that the minister continue his remarks?
Agreed.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I see that the quality of mercy is not strained. I appreciate the courtesy I have been shown and I do not intend to trespass upon it.
The second section of interest concerns the right of appeal being restricted. The third one is whether adequate facilities exist in Canada for the economic production of such goods within a reasonable period of time. Of course, that is an involved sentence and could be subject to various interpretations.
I am not going to suggest for a moment that there is not some room for debate as to what is a reasonable period of time. If you are making a thermal generator, which takes three years to build, or tin cans-
What about a 2J cubic yards shovel?
-or if you are making a shovel, which takes a month-
It took in that case five years.

We can also argue the five-year period but we are not going to do that. Those are the three limited areas in which the power is vested in the minister. The right of appeal still exists in the major field.
It has been suggested that the right of appeal will be taken away by this bill. The right of appeal exists. Also, a great deal of

play has been made of the word "approximately". There is an appeal on whether goods are of approximately a class or kind which has been made in Canada before.
With regard to the determination of Canadian production, as I said a moment ago when referring to the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate, there can be no hole-in-the-corner and no arrangement can be made with your friends, as has been suggested, because in that area there is an appeal to the tariff board and again to the courts. Of course, with regard to whether Canadian consumption is actually 10 per cent or more there is also a right of appeal.
I am sorry, Mr. Chairman, to have taken up so much time, but we have been sitting here for some little while debating this subject and I thought I would be pardoned if I tried to bring this matter into perspective as I see it and as I think, frankly, the Canadian public see it and anyone who has dealings with the department.
I am very proud of the department. I think the departmental officials are recognized by everyone in Canada as being men of ability. The senior officials are recognized as being men of experience and integrity, with a record of service which is unequalled by any other department in this country or elsewhere. To suggest that these matters could be manipulated in any way, shape or form is rather difficult for me to accept.
I hope I have not transgressed the rule of good nature to which I tried to adhere myself with some difficulty when I started and that having had this discussion we can now proceed to pass this bill.
I say again that the amendments which are proposed are rather important. In so far as concerns the extension of the minister's powers by the use of the word "approximately", and extending the type of goods which have not been made in Canada before but for which the economic and productive capacity is here, this is a rather limited area in a field in which the Department of National Revenue has been actively administering for half a century. I suggest that the country and this committee can leave these matters for decision by the department, because after all the final appeal is to this supreme court.
Is the decision made by a junior clerk, or yourself?

This is the supreme court of Canada, and no one can suggest for one moment that it is not. If there were any of the suggested derelictions of duty which have been put forward with exaggerated emphasis by hon. gentlemen in the debate on this bill, they would appear before this house within a month of their occurring. Here is the final

right of appeal given to the Canadian people, and I am sure they will not find that this section has been abused to the extent, or in any way such as has been suggested during this debate.

Mr. Chairman, I will take only a minute to attempt to deal with the minister's last remarks. We have heard from the minister a moving and indeed impassioned appeal. He will forgive me if I say that I am not impressed. Perhaps I had better put it this way; I was certainly impressed by the facility of his language, but I was not impressed by the logic of his argument, because for most of his speech the minister dealt with administrative decisions from which there is not an appeal now and has not been in the past.
We are dealing now with matters from which in the past there has been an appeal. That appeal is now being taken away by legislation. The minister may say that these matters are, the word he used in connection with one of them was infinitesimal in importance. However, we are dealing with matters of trade and business which may reach $250 million.
However important or unimportant these matters may be-and we think they are important-the fact remains that an appeal has existed from decisions in respect of them in the past and this government, by legislation, is now taking away that right of appeal. No eloquence on the part of the minister can deny that fact.
The minister says these matters are not important and should not cause any anxiety in our minds. The minister says that he and his department can be trusted to administer these matters. We have great respect for the minister's ability and sincerity, and we have great respect for the officials of his department.
However, the fact cannot be denied that something which has existed in the past in the way of an appeal to the tariff board and to the court is now being taken away. That is why so much anxiety has been created not only in the minds of the hon. members of the opposition but throughout the country. That anxiety and worry on the part of the people of this country has been expressed by us in the house, and no eloquence of the minister will be able to deny that fact.
No eloquence on the part of the minister and no effort on his part to read all the decisions on which there is no appeal can deny the fact that an appeal has existed over the years and that appeal is now being taken away by legislation.

Mr. Chairman, the minister said something about this house
Customs Tariff
being the supreme court of Canada. I should like to remind the minister that the only area in which this house has been the supreme court is in the case of divorces, and it is even running into road blocks there.
The minister is a very able man. In fact, the minister is one of the most eloquent speakers I have listened to for a long time. He can successfully pull wool over the eyes of almost anyone. I happen to be in the fortunate position where I have not much wool which can be pulled over my eyes and the minister cannot do this to me.
The minister talked about the possibility of capricious appeals. There is certainly the possibility of capricious appeals. But is there not also the possibility of a capricious minister if we give him all the power that is involved in this bill? I will not say the possibility is there now. I am not accusing the minister of anything. However, we have to look ahead. When bills are passed they become the law until such time as they are revoked at some future date.
There is another aspect of this matter which rather concerns me. The minister referred to it two or three times. I refer to the remarks of the minister when he said that the government has had to put up with a debate on this subject for a period of seven or eight days. I should like to warn the minister that he is treading on very dangerous territory and would suggest that he think-twice before taking a step such as this bill proposes. If this proposes nothing new, as the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Trade and Commerce have said, then why should we be asked to pass it? Surely there must be something new involved here or it would not be before the committee at this time.
I should like to mention one other matter which comes to mind as a result of the wording of this proposed amendment. I had intended to move an amendment so similar to this that I should like to read it for purposes of comparison. The amendment I proposed was that Bill No. C-72 be amended by removing the whole of section 3 of subsection 2A. It is the experience of this group that any time we find ourselves as close as this in thought to the Liberals we have cause for grave concern and have to search our souls to make sure that we are on the right path.
Would you be interested in knowing that the concern is mutual?

We have learned from the hard lessons of history during the 94 years that this country has been in existence that we have no more reason to trust the Liberals than the Tories, and vice

Customs Tariff
versa. They are six of one and half a dozen of the other as far as we are concerned.
I do not think he even trusts himself.
I would ask the minister whether he would be happy to place such trust in a C.C.F. minister granted these powers?
No, no.
If the answer is no, then why should he-
That is hypothetically ridiculous.

Why should he place such powers in the hands of a Liberal or Tory minister? There is one difference between this party and others in this regard, and that is we would not give this power to even a C.C.F. minister if we were the government.
That would be even worse.

There is no place in a democracy for the granting of power in the way proposed by this bill, without any recourse to appeal. There is no place in a democracy for a provision of this kind, and that is why we support this amendment.

Mr. Chairman, the Minister of National Revenue was indeed very careful not to refer directly to anything I said in the hope that I would not reply to his argument. That is a vain hope because I intend to clear up one point at once. I said that a minister under this legislation could do certain things. I did not at any time suggest or insinuate in any way that the present minister would do those things. I am sure the minister will agree with me in that. I do say it is a wrong and unsound principle of government to trust even the most able and upright minister. I should like to quote again from what the right hon. gentleman, who is now the Prime Minister of Canada, said when he was over on this side of the house in 1950 with regard to this precise point. The Prime Minister is reported to have said:
-and if we are to accept at face value what ministers say, we had better all be absent from this house.
Those words of the Prime Minister ought to be remembered by all members supporting this bill, because it was on the basis of this kind of statement, and on the basis of specious arguments that were made by hon. gentlemen who are now on the treasury benches about their predecessors there, that the Prime Minister made his appeal to the country and

got into office. It does seem to me to be most extraordinary that the same gentleman, when on this side said:
If the cabinet is to be trusted and if we are to accept at face value what ministers say, we had better all be absent from this house.
The Prime Minister is now absent looking after the affairs of other countries than his own.
Oh, oh.
That is precisely what he is doing.
Shame.

I suggest that anyone who read the account of what the Prime Minister had to say today, as it appeared in the newspapers, would see that he was telling other countries how to run their affairs. I suggest that the Prime Minister has a more urgent task, and that is to deal with the way in which the affairs of this country are being mismanaged. That is what he was elected to do, manage the affairs of this country, not give lectures to other countries.
That is not worthy of you.

I say that if the cabinet is to be trusted, as the Prime Minister said, and if we are to accept at face value what ministers say, we had better all be absent from this house. Yet the gentleman who said that now asks us to trust not just the cabinet, but a single minister and as my hon. friend the Leader of the Opposition said, to trust a single minister in something which heretofore has been subject to appeal.
This bill proposes the taking away of a right. It does not seem to me that it makes any difference whether there are 64 or 6,400 cases in the statutes where there is no right of appeal and never has been. I think the minister will have great difficulty in finding one single case where a right of appeal, which has hitherto existed, has been taken away by this parliament. Surely, the point is that a right of appeal which now exists is being taken away; that which exists now will no longer exist. Notwithstanding the bill of rights, a right which a subject now has will no longer exist if this bill receives royal assent.
I have only one other point to make in regard to the amendment put forward by the hon. member for Ottawa West. It seemed to me that the Minister of National Revenue made a very weak argument indeed when he pointed out that Mr. Bennett provided a tribunal separate from the Department of National Revenue in respect to these appeals. I feel that was a forward step, but I wonder

why this government wants to undo, in some respects, what Mr. Bennett did. The minister has suggested, and I think rightly so, that Mr. Bennett set up a tariff board creating a right of appeal outside the department which had not before existed. When Mr. Bennett's successor came into office that right of appeal was made more complete and precise. This was done by the legislation brought forward in 1936 by Mr. Dunning. The whole trend has been to permit appeals and extend the area of them. This bill, which seeks to undo this, is turning back the clock. As my hon. friend, the Leader of the Opposition, has pointed out, these are not insignificant matters. These are matters which may involve one quarter of a billion dollars' worth of business. These are matters which may affect the profitability of our export industries and their capacity to improve their capital structure. These surely are not insignificant matters, however much the minister may say they are.

I think many hon. members now sitting in this committee will recall that I protested with some vehemence last week with regard to a tendency that I thought had been developed by the ministry in presenting information to parliament after the opportunity for debate had been concluded. The particular instance to which I refer was the presentation of a document after the time when members of parliament would normally have it brought to their attention, and after debate had concluded in respect of a particular item in the estimates of the Department of Agriculture. I recall the jeers of last week with respect to this item. Hon. members thought perhaps I was not attentive, or something of that nature.
I wish to refer to notice of motion No. 50, which was a request for copies of orders issued by the Minister of National Revenue since December 1, 1958, under provisions of section 38 of the Customs Act. I wish to pay my personal tribute to the Minister of National Revenue who told me today that return to this order had been tabled. I appreciate that courtesy, but other members of parliament would not know about the tabling of this document until tomorrow when they received Votes and Proceedings, which are the minutes of the proceedings of the House of Commons. Only then would they have been alerted as to what was available to the public and to our colleagues in the house in connection with the business of the house.
In connection with the report of the grain growers association which was referred to by the Toronto Telegram, I wish to repeat that not one member out of the 261 in this house could possibly have known about the availability of the report until the day after the debate had concluded in the house. In
Customs Tariff
this instance, having regard to the matter before us and section 38 of the Customs Act, I thank the minister for drawing the tabling of this document to my attention.
When a committee of this house was set up in 1959, following amendments to the Customs Act in 1958, there was no difficulty whatsoever in providing the estimates committee of this house within a matter of two or three days with a complete list of all orders that had been issued under the new legislation of 1958. I say it is a travesty of the rights of members of parliament, who are seeking information, to receive, despite the courtesy of the Minister of National Revenue, information at the last moment. I would not have known until tomorrow, when Votes and Proceedings are published, had it not been for the courtesy of the minister, what was tabled today in the House of Commons. I refer to material which relates to this debate and to the provisions of section 38 of the Customs Act, which was amended in radical form in 1958 by the new government. I appeal to all on the opposite side not to continue this kind of thing. I want to assure them that to the extent that I am capable I will be alert to all kinds of offences of this nature. I referred to some of them when I spoke last week. This is not treating the opposition as they should be treated and I do not think that the Minister of Finance, who is looking askance, the Minister of National Revenue, or anybody else, despite their oratory in past days, will ever find examples of parliament being ignored to the extent that the opposition has been ignored in the past. After all, the opposition is a component of parliament.
As I say, my return was tabled this afternoon. Other members would not know anything about it were it not for the courtesy of the Minister of National Revenue who indicated to me privately that it had been tabled with the Clerk of the House of Commons. Only tomorrow would members of parliament generally learn that the return had been made.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Is the committee ready for the question?
Amendment (Mr. Mcllraith) negatived: Yeas, 27; nays, 66.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I declare the amendment lost.

Mr. Chairman, there is one point that I want to deal with rather briefly. It has to do with the term "custom made to specifications" in clause 2A(l)(a). There seems to me to be a lack of clarity in the language, and I think the Minister of National Revenue rather pointed it up in his own

Customs Tariff
remarks. It seems to me the reference should be to "user's specifications", so that paragraph (a) would read:
In the case of goods other than goods custom-made to user's specifications.
And so on.
Surely, the phrase "custom made to specif-, ications" should have some further definition in it. Whose specifications? Surely, this should be clarified. I admit it is a small point, but it should be dealt with and I propose moving an amendment adding the word "user's". If I put the amendment formally before the committee, then it will limit the discussion to the narrow point. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate:
That paragraph (a) of subsection 1 of section 2A be amended by adding the word "user's" in line 10 before the word "specifications".
It would seem to be obvious that if this amendment carries appropriate amendments would have to be made to the other subsections but if it is defeated there would perhaps be no need to cover the ground again.

Mr. Chairman, I cannot see anything wrong with the insertion of the word "user's" except that in many cases the specifications are the property of the manufacturer and he is simply meeting a condition of the customer. They are the manufacturer's specifications. There may be modifications to these specifications which are required because of peculiar circumstances with respect to the site, operating conditions or what not, but in very few cases would they be the user's specifications. I can understand the intent of the amendment and I can see that it would perhaps apply to such things as automatic transmissions where the specifications are those of the user, the automobile manufacturing company. If there are facilities in this country for manufacturing such items then the phrase "user's specifications" would be appropriate and I would be all in favour of such a change. However, having a little knowledge of the engineering and machinery field, it seems to me that the amendment would do more to confuse than to help. Although the amendment has merit, in my opinion it would be too limiting.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a brief comment. Normally the specifications that are contemplated by the bill would be user's specifications but there may be cases where the specifications are not those of the user. They may be those of the producer, just as the hon. member for Vancouver South has indicated. If it were not for this fact, one would be glad to meet the point raised by the hon. member for Ottawa West. The fact is there may be cases

where the specifications are not those of the user although normally that would be the case. For that reason, I think it would be unwise to limit this provision in the bill.

I should like to ask the
Minister of Finance one question on that point. I take it this provision will mean that the manufacturer in Canada can allege that goods are custom made to specifications when in fact they are shelf goods. Surely that was never intended, but as I see it that could be one possibility. It seems to me a more precise definition is required than simply "custom made to specifications". I am not arguing particularly that it should be limited to user's specifications but surely it cannot be left open so anyone can say that it is the specifications of the manufacturer of competitive goods or something of that nature. Surely there must be some tying down of the specifications to some person or group of persons. That is my point.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not follow the hon. member in his reasoning, either in his reference to shelf goods or in what he has last said. He is overlooking the fact, I think, that there may be a great deal of engineering work to be done in these situations. The user, the intending purchaser, indicates his problem. He does not lay down hard and fast specifications himself but rather indicates his problem. The manufacturer will then contribute not only the goods but the design and he takes full responsibility for a design to meet the particular need indicated by the intending user. In that case the specifications are not laid down by the user. They are the manufacturer's specifications.
May I ask a question at that point? Does the design not become a design that the user has procured? It is the user's design at that point although the manufacturer has provided it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, that is where I think the hon. member is in error.

That is the very point. The user may provide the specifications himself or he may procure them from another firm and it may be that the very firm which is to manufacture the equipment will provide them. However, surely they are still the user's specifications. Surely, something more precise than the present language is required.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am sorry, I do not follow the hon. member and I cannot agree with him.

Mr. Chairman, when we can afford it the minister and I buy new suits and we buy them from swatches that

may involve importation from a British woollen manufacturing company. I do not know whether that is desirable-
Very desirable.

-but I want to know what the officials think who are sitting in front of the minister tonight with respect to whether the ordering of a woollen worsted suit under such circumstances is considered to be an ordering of shelf goods-as far as I know the goods are not on the shelf when the suit is ordered here in Canada-or whether it is a custom made order. How is the administration likely to administer this kind of provision? People may laugh but this is a very important matter. With all our respect for civil servants, we are giving bureaucrats rights under this bill that are not subject to any appeal in the traditional way to the tariff board, the Exchequer Court of Canada or the Supreme Court of Canada.
I do not want to draw attention to my suit but let us say that a small swatch of suiting has been created in Great Britain for use as a sample in Canada. I am persuaded that the particular pattern is not run off for everybody. They only run off a few yards in order to have possibly 12 inch by 12 inch samples. After their agents have travelled throughout the world and obtained orders, they may then decide on a reasonable run of this suiting in order to fill the orders that have been received.
In such cases there would be a delay of six to nine months from the time of creation of the first small run and I should like the minister to tell me whether or not Canada is going to regard these suitings as shelf goods. In my view they are not on the shelf, but are importers of such goods going to be regarded as importing custom made goods?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Except for the dumping duty, there is nothing in this bill that has any bearing whatever upon suitings.
I am not going to be put off in that way. I know that on December 20 the minister asserted that there were no rate increases provided here. He stands on that position.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is no textile item involved.

The parliamentary secretary is quite right. There is no specific increase provided in respect of any individual item among the thousands we have in the Customs Tariff. However, as a result of parliament adopting this bill we will find, as we found during the Bennett regime, increases in the amounts of duty by tremendous percentages. There is no question about that. I know
Customs Tariff
that the committee does not want me to repeat the quotations I gave yesterday from reliable sources.
I want to say that there are two things involved here. There is a direct opportunity for the tariff administration in national revenue to make an assessment under the made in Canada or not made in Canada provision. I suggest the department is going to make many decisions in the future that such and such a product is the equivalent of that made in Canada and, as a result, the department will have the right to invoke dumping duties. Otherwise, they have no right to refer to dumping duties.
I want to emphasize to all members of this committee that every student of tariffs has said that he requires no final statute, he requires nothing in the Custom Tariff if he has what was given to this government in 1958 in the way of ministerial discretion. The tariff board has been enlarged. It was said that the final judgments of the board would be worthy and helpful in influencing the administration with regard to recommendations for changes in the tariff schedule. I repeat that from now on if the minister of national revenue has the powers granted by this bill added to the powers given by the bill in 1958, any recommendations from the tariff board, after thoughtful and deliberate discussion, will be a farce.
Amendment (Mr. Mcllraith) negatived: Yeas, 25; nays, 71.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I declare the amendment lost.

I do not intend to detain the committee with any speech, but since the first amendment moved by the hon. member for Ottawa West has been rejected and it would, therefore, be improper to enter again into an argument on that amendment, I merely wish to say that since the committee has decided it will not recommend to the house that subsection 3 of the section be taken out, I move:
That a new subsection 4 be added to section 2A as follows:
(4) Any ruling made under this section shall be published forthwith in the Canada Gazette.
It does seem to me, sir, if we are not going to permit an appeal at least we should make a provision for publicity so that everyone will know what is happening. This does not mean that anything more than the ruling itself needs to be published. However, at least there would be a means for the members of this house, and for everyone, to know what the government was, in fact, doing.

I do not believe the members of the committee are familiar with the

Customs Tariff
fact that for many years a very fine periodical has been published by the Department of National Revenue under the title, "Made in Canada Rulings". This is the normal procedure of the Minister of National Revenue, and the rulings relate to what is considered to be made in Canada and what is not made in Canada. I think the minister should tell us to what extent these new amendments will avoid publicizing a decision in the way it has always been publicized. I will give an example. I have here series "D", decision No. 51, dated October 23, 1953, relating to gasoline engine driven fork lift trucks. Precise details are given as to what fork lift trucks are made in Canada and what fork lift trucks are not made in Canada. I think henceforth we in this committee want to know the intention of the Minister of National Revenue in this respect. In respect of a certain article he will reach a decision that it is going to be regarded as possibly being made in Canada and that the tariff rate will be 22J per cent vis-a-vis the United States instead of 7-J per cent, I think it is, if it was not an article made in Canada.
The point here to which I wish to draw the attention of the Minister of Finance is this. In fairness to everybody across Canada there should be knowledge of what is going to be done. Inasmuch as it has been traditional for these rulings to be made public, what is the intention of the minister? Members of parliament may think we are asking for something that is unusual. However, this is something that has gone out every day in the week in the past. I refer to rulings with respect to what has been made in Canada and what has not been made in Canada, with definitive descriptions of the article involved. I want to know whether, under the new legislation, the Minister of National Revenue is likely to continue that form of advice to all interested in these trades so that, if he makes a decision under the laws that have been passed today, all people will be treated equally.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
First, may I point out what the situation is at the present time. Class or kind rulings are all made at the head office of the department here in Ottawa. These rulings are public, although not in the sense that they are today published in the Canada Gazette. Copies of the rulings are available to anyone today. Certainly there has been no thought at any time on the part of the government that rulings made under this bill, when enacted, would not be available to the public.
The hon. member's amendment contemplates the addition of a subclause 4 and it reads as follows:

Any ruling made under this section shall be published forthwith in the Canada Gazette.
I had thought that what the hon. member was principally concerned with was the kind of rulings to be made which become final under subclause 3.
That is right.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If that is what he has in mind in connection with this amendment, I think we can quickly find ourselves on common ground if he will be prepared to alter the proposed language of the new clause 4 to read after this fashion:
Any decision of the minister with respect to the matters enumerated in subsection 3 shall be published forthwith in the Canada Gazette.

That amendment will be completely satisfactory to me. I should be very happy to incorporate it in the language the Minister of Finance has just used. It seems to me that is precisely the point. We feel that there should be a certainty in the law that these findings under subsection 3 will be published. I am happy indeed that the Minister of Finance has seen fit to accept this suggestion, I do not pretend to be a legal draftsman and I am very happy to accept the suggestion.

I, too, thank the Minister of Finance for his acceptance of this advice. I think this means that all in a certain industry are likely to know of ministerial decisions that are made possible by this subsection 3.

I wish very briefly on behalf of this group to say that, while we frequently question the wisdom of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, in this case we think he has demonstrated some good common sense in putting forward this amendment and we intend to support it. We are also glad to note that the minister has agreed to accept it and that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has agreed to accept the minister's suggestion with respect to the slight amendment. We believe it is a good thing for the actions of the government under this bill to come into the light of day so that the public will know what is being done. At the same time I think the inclusion of this amendment in the bill will make the government conscious of the fact that the public, or the section of the public that is particularly concerned, will know of the the minister's actions in the administration of this act. While the minister mentioned that there are other means or ways of getting this information or that it is obtainable from other sources, we think that the Canada Gazette is the proper medium through which to inform the public of the government's decisions in this respect.

Before concluding my brief remarks I might say that I am under the impression that there must be some mental telepathy on this side of the house because we have been thinking of this matter for some time. That has affected the mind of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. We are extremely pleased on that account.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
So that we may have the amendment in written form, Mr. Chairman, may I say that this is what I have drafted, if it is acceptable to the hon. member who has moved the amendment. The proposed clause 4 to be added would now read as follows:
Any decision of the minister with respect to the matters enumerated in subsection 3 hereof shall be published forthwith in the Canada Gazette.
That is completely satisfactory to me.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: STATES FOR AVOIDANCE OF DOUBLE TAXATION
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-82, to implement a convention between
Estate Tax
Canada and the United States of America for the avoidance of double taxation and the prevention of fiscal evasion with respect to taxes on the estates of deceased persons.
He said: Mr. Speaker, on February 17 I announced to the house, as recorded at page 2145 of Hansard, that an estate tax convention had been concluded between Canada and the United States. The convention was signed in Washington on that day.
Hon. members may be interested to know that this was the first treaty signed by the new United States administration, just as the Columbia river treaty was the last treaty signed by the retiring administration. The purpose of Bill No. C-82 is to implement this convention.
In my statement of February 17 1 described in general terms the purposes and effects of the convention. I do not propose to repeat the comments which I then made. I may remind hon. members that the convention is in addition to the existing Canada-United States convention of 1944 which continues to apply to the estates of persons who died before January 1, 1959.
The new convention applies to the estates of persons dying on or after that date, which is the date on which the Canadian Estate Tax Act superseded the Dominion Succession Duty Act. The convention follows the general pattern of the 1944 convention between Canada and the United States and the conventions between Canada and the United Kingdom, France, Ireland and South Africa. Certain desirable changes have, however, been made.
The convention is attached to the bill as a schedule thereto. The bill itself, in both substance and form, is familiar to hon. members who have in recent years perused a good many bills to approve and implement tax conventions. Since the convention, if approved by parliament, would prevail over the Estate Tax Act in the event of any inconsistency, care has been taken in drafting the convention to insure that the taxpayer secures any relief to which he is entitled under the convention without losing any advantage to which he may be entitled under the ordinary law.
The convention will not come into force until it receives legislative approval in both countries and certain formalities are completed. When it comes into force it will be retroactive to January 1, 1959 so as to provide continuity with the existing succession duty convention. Consequently benefits resulting from its terms will apply to the estates of persons dying on or after January 1, 1959.
Mr. Speaker, I think I may reserve my

Estate Tax
comments on the major articles of the convention until we are in committee on the bill. I recall that on such measures in times past, because of the fact that they follow a well established pattern, the discussion has been largely confined to the committee stage.
Mr. W. M. Benidickson (Kenora-Rainy
River): Mr. Speaker, we are fast approaching the adjournment hour of ten o'clock. This bill involves some technicalities with which I assume very few hon. members of the house are familiar. I confess I am not too familiar with them, although we all participated in the revision of the Canadian Estate Tax Act in 1959, I think it was.
I recall that fairly long and interesting discussions that took place at that time in the banking and commerce committee of this house. I take it that as a result of a rather wholesale revision of Canada's system with respect to the estates of deceased persons, including persons with United States residence who might have a liability, this particular legislation is necessary.
I imagine that having regard to the technicalities involved the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) would be very pleased to accede to my request that we call it ten o'clock. I take it that this does not in any way involve another legislative act that we must pass in the House of Commons relating to a United States-Canadian tax treaty because of the minister's supplementary budget
of December. I take it this measure relates only to taxation with respect to deceased persons.
I see it is ten o'oclock. I am sure the Minister of Finance will agree-and I see that the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) agrees-that we could discuss this legislation at another opportunity.
Mr. Speaker, before you leave the chair perhaps the house leader will tell us, so it will be on Hansard, what is proposed for the rest of the week.
